### 1.1 Before listening (2 minutes, Arabic is fine here)

1. What have you learned without a teacher?
2. How long have you studied English?
3. Is there something you started and have not finished yet?

### 1.4 Now read the passage

### Passage: *One Small Thing, Many Times* (400 words)

Lina is twenty-four. She lives in Gaza, and she has studied information technology at her college for three years. She has also done something her teachers never asked for: she has taught herself web design.

**[A]** It started two years ago, with a free course on the internet. The course has more than forty lessons, and Lina has finished thirty-eight of them. She has never met her teacher. He lives in another country, and she has only seen his hands, moving on a keyboard, in short videos.

The connection in her building is slow, so she has learned to work in a careful way. She downloads a lesson at night, when the internet is quieter. She watches it in the morning, with no connection at all. She has lost her work many times, and now she saves every few minutes.

**[B]** Her uncle has a small shop near the market. He has sold the same things for twenty years — bags, shoes, school things — and he has always sold them in the same way. People come to the shop, or they telephone him.

In March, Lina built a website for the shop. It is a simple one: four pages, some photographs, the prices, and a button that opens a message to her uncle's phone. She published it on a free service, because the shop has no money for anything else. It took her eleven days.

**[C]** Since March, the shop has had customers from three other cities. They have never seen the shop, and they will probably never see it. They found the website, they looked at the prices, and they sent a message. Two of them have ordered from the shop more than once.

Her uncle has not learned to use a computer, and he does not want to. He has never used email. But he has asked Lina for two new pages, and he has started to say "my website" when he talks to his friends.

**[D]** Lina has not finished the course yet. Two lessons are left, and they are the hardest ones. She has already decided what she will build after them: an account system, so that a customer can see what he has ordered before.

She says the same thing to every student who asks her how to begin. "I have not done anything big," she says. "I have done one small thing, many times, for two years".

### 1.5 Read aloud

Read the passage aloud **once** and record it. Compare it with your Lesson 3 recording: is the voice steadier now?

parts.title: Grammar — the present perfect
parts.markdown:
We use the present perfect when the past still touches now: *She **has built** a website* — and the website is there today.

### 3.1 How we make it

**have / has** + the **past participle**

| Person | Present perfect |
|---|---|
| I / you / we / they | **have** finished |
| he / she / it | **has** finished |

The past participle of a regular verb is the *-ed* form you already know. The common irregular ones must be learned:

| Now | Past participle |
|---|---|
| be | **been** |
| do | **done** |
| see | **seen** |
| take | **taken** |
| build | **built** |
| lose | **lost** |
| sell | **sold** |
| meet | **met** |
| pay | **paid** |
| finish | finish**ed** *(regular)* |
| learn | learn**ed** *(regular)* |
| decide | decid**ed** *(regular)* |

### 3.2 What we use it for

- **Experience**, at any time in your life: *She **has never met** her teacher.*
- Something that **started in the past and is still true**: *He **has sold** the same things for twenty years.*
- A past action with a **result now**: *She **has lost** her work many times, so now she saves every few minutes.*
- With **for** and **since**: ***for*** + a length of time (*for two years*), ***since*** + a point in time (*since March*).

### 3.4 Present perfect or past simple?

| Past simple — finished time | Present perfect — unfinished, or the result now |
|---|---|
| *In March*, she **built** a website. | *Since March*, the shop **has had** new customers. |
| She **published** it on a free service. | She **has not finished** the course yet. |
| It **took** her eleven days. | He **has sold** the same things for twenty years. |

The rule to remember: if the sentence says **when** it happened and that time is over (*in March, two years ago, yesterday*), use the past simple. If it says **for**, **since**, **yet**, **already**, **ever** or **never**, use the present perfect.

### 3.5 Negative and question

|  | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Negative | **have not / has not** + participle | He **has not learned** to use a computer. |
| Question | **Have / Has** + person + participle | **Has** she **finished** the course? |

### 3.6 Grammar practice

**A. Put the verb in the present perfect:**

1. Lina \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (study) at her college for three years.
2. She \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (never / meet) her teacher.
3. The shop \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (have) customers from other cities since March.
4. She \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (not finish) the course yet.
5. He \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (already / ask) for two new pages.
6. They \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (never / see) the shop.

**B. Past simple or present perfect?**

1. In March, she (built / has built) a website.
2. Since March, the shop (had / has had) new customers.
3. She (published / has published) it on a free service.
4. She (did not finish / has not finished) the course yet.
5. Her uncle (sold / has sold) the same things for twenty years.

**C. Write *for* or *since*:**

1. \_\_\_\_ three years
2. \_\_\_\_ March
3. \_\_\_\_ twenty years
4. \_\_\_\_ she was a child

parts.title: The short forms of have and has
parts.markdown: ### 3.3 The short forms of *have* and *has* (listen to `05-have-has-forms.mp3`) In speech, *have* and *has* are almost never said in full. They join the word before them and become very short. This is why the present perfect is hard to **hear** even when it is easy to write. | Full | Short form | Sound | |---|---|---| | I have | I've | /aɪv/ | | you have | you've | /juːv/ | | they have | they've | /ðeɪv/ | | he has | he's | /hiːz/ | | she has | she's | /ʃiːz/ | | it has | it's | /ɪts/ | | have not | haven't | /ˈhævənt/ | | has not | hasn't | /ˈhæzənt/ | Inside a sentence, a full *have* or *has* is also weak and quiet: /həv/ and /həz/, not /hæv/ and /hæz/. ### The one that catches everybody ***she's*** is two different words. | You hear | It means | How you know | |---|---|---| | *She's **finished** the course.* | she **has** finished | a past participle comes after it | | *She's **a student**.* | she **is** a student | a noun or an adjective comes after it | The word **after** *she's* tells you which one it is. The same is true of *he's* and *it's*. In the audio you hear each pair twice — the full form, then the short one — and then a test: say whether the *'s* you hear means **has** or **is**, and listen to the answer.

segments.say: Pronunciation. The short forms of have and has.
In speech, have and has are almost never said in full. They join the word before them and become very short. Listen to each pair: first the full form, then the short one. Repeat the short one.
They have never seen the shop.
He has not learned to use a computer.
He hasn't learned to use a computer.
Now the hard one. She's can mean she has, or she is. The word after it tells you. If a past participle comes next, it means has. If a noun or an adjective comes next, it means is.
You will hear a sentence. Say whether the short form means has or is. Then you will hear the answer.
She's a student at the college.
He's sold the same things for twenty years.
This is the end of the pronunciation practice.

parts.title: Comprehension — TOEFL question types
parts.markdown:
### Part A — Multiple choice

**1. (Factual)** What has Lina taught herself?

- A. Information technology.
- B. Web design.
- C. Photography.
- D. The passage does not say.

**2. (Factual)** How long has her uncle sold the same things?

- A. For two years.
- B. For eleven days.
- C. For twenty years.
- D. Since March.

**3. (Negative factual)** According to the passage, Lina has done all of the following EXCEPT

- A. finished thirty-eight lessons.
- B. built a website for the shop.
- C. met her teacher.
- D. lost her work many times.

**4. (Vocabulary in context)** The word "published" in the passage is closest in meaning to

- A. printed on paper.
- B. put on the internet.
- C. sold to a customer.
- D. kept in a folder.

**5. (Reference)** In the sentence, she published it on a free service, the word "it" refers to

- A. the course.
- B. the shop.
- C. the website.
- D. the message.

**6. (Inference)** It can be inferred from the passage that

- A. Lina's uncle has learned web design from her.
- B. the slow connection has changed the way Lina works.
- C. the shop has closed since March.
- D. Lina will stop the course after thirty-eight lessons.

**7. (Sentence insertion)** Look at the four letters **[A] [B] [C] [D]** in the passage. Where would this sentence best fit?

> *The whole thing has cost the shop nothing at all.*

- A. At **[A]**
- B. At **[B]**
- C. At **[C]**
- D. At **[D]**

**8. (Purpose of a paragraph)** Why does the writer mention that Lina downloads a lesson at night?

- A. To show that she prefers working at night.
- B. To show how she has worked around a slow connection.
- C. To explain why she has never met her teacher.
- D. To criticise the internet company.

**9. (Purpose of the whole passage — NEW)** What is the writer's main purpose in the whole passage?

- A. To explain how to build a website.
- B. To show that small work, repeated over a long time, produces a real result.
- C. To advertise a free online course.
- D. To describe daily life in Gaza.

parts.title: Writing — Something I Have Done, Step by Step
parts.markdown:
### 5.2 Writing — "Something I Have Done, Step by Step" (12–14 sentences)

**Model answer (copy the shape, change the words):**

> I have studied English for four years. I started at school, and I was not good at it. Three years ago, I began to study alone, because my class was too fast for me. I have used free videos on the internet since then. I have finished more than two hundred short lessons. I have never paid for a course. At first, I understood almost nothing, and I wrote every new word in a small notebook. Now I have four notebooks, and I read the old ones on Fridays. I have not finished yet. I still make mistakes with tenses, and I have never spoken to a person from England. But my teacher has said that my writing has changed this year. It is slow work, and it is the only work that has helped me.

**Checklist before you send it:**

- [ ] I used the present perfect at least **four** times.
- [ ] I used the past simple for the things that happened at a finished time.
- [ ] I used **for** with a length of time and **since** with a point in time.
- [ ] I used *not … yet*, *already* or *never* at least once.
- [ ] I used at least **5 new words** from Session 2.
- [ ] I used at least **2 words** from Lesson 2 or Lesson 3.
- [ ] My text has 12–14 sentences.

parts.markdown:
**Listening:** L1 — Lina; she has taught herself web design · L2 — for three years · L3 — a website, for her uncle's shop · L4 — no, she has not finished it yet (two lessons are left)

**Part A (MCQ):** 1-B · 2-C · 3-C · 4-B · 5-C · 6-B · 7-C · 8-B · 9-B

*Why 7 is **[C]***: the sentence is about cost, and it can only follow the paragraph that says the site was published on a free service because the shop has no money. At **[B]** and **[D]** there is no cost in the text near it.

*Why 8 is **[B]***: downloading at night is an example of working around the slow connection named in the sentence before it. It is not about preference, and the teacher is in a different paragraph.

*Why 9 is **[B]***: the passage is not instructions, and it is not about Gaza in general. Every part of it — thirty-eight lessons, eleven days, one small shop — builds to Lina's own last line about doing one small thing many times.

**Part B (True/False):**

1. F — She has finished thirty-eight lessons; two are left.
2. T
3. F — He has not learned to use a computer.
4. T
5. F — They have never seen the shop.
6. T

**Part C (Fill in the blanks):** 1. course · 2. connection · 3. website · 4. prices · 5. published · 6. customers · 7. account
*(Extra words: online, password)*

**2.4 A (Opposites):** 1. expensive · 2. offline · 3. hide / keep private · 4. seller / shopkeeper · 5. finish / end

**2.4 B (Odd one out):** 1. market (the others are parts of the internet) · 2. password (the others belong to a shop) · 3. free (the others are past-simple verbs)

**3.6 A (Present perfect):** 1. has studied · 2. has never met · 3. has had · 4. has not finished · 5. has already asked · 6. have never seen
**3.6 B (Simple or perfect):** 1. built · 2. has had · 3. published · 4. has not finished · 5. has sold
**3.6 C (for / since):** 1. for · 2. since · 3. for · 4. since

**Mini-quiz:** 1. built · 2. lost · 3. seen · 4. for, since · 5. expensive · 6. offline · 7. website · 8. customer · 9–12. teacher judgement

### Teacher Notes {: #teacher-notes }

**What changed from Lesson 3.** The passage grew from 320 to 400 words, the present perfect joins the past simple and the past continuous, and an eighth question type — the purpose of the whole passage — closes the set. The pronunciation slot follows the grammar again, as it has since Lesson 2: the three sounds of *-ed*, then the weak *was* and *were*, now the short forms of *have* and *has*. Everything else is deliberately unchanged.

**The one real difficulty.** Not the form. It is choosing between *I did* and *I have done*, and Arabic gives no help: both land on the same past. The test is whether the sentence names a finished time. Drill 3.4 and 3.6 B until *in March* pulls the past simple and *since March* pulls the present perfect without thought. Expect *I have built it in March* for several weeks, and correct it every time.

**Why the listening matters more this week.** *Have* and *has* almost disappear in speech. A student who can write *she has finished* will still hear *she's finished* as *she's finish*, and then lose the tense entirely. That is the reason part 05 exists, and the reason the *she's* table is on the sheet: the word after the contraction is the only clue, and she has to learn to use it.

**Why this story.** It is the first passage with no disaster in it. Lessons 1 to 3 were a slow internet, a lost phone and a power cut — real, but if every passage is a loss the course starts teaching helplessness. This one is about a person whose work accumulated, which is also the honest description of what this course asks of her. The vocabulary is the vocabulary of putting your own work in front of other people: publish, account, customer, update.

**Success criteria for Lesson 4.** The student should be able to:

- answer L1–L4 correctly on the second hearing;
- hear *she's finished* and say whether it means *has* or *is*;
- form the present perfect of ten verbs, including five irregular participles;
- choose correctly between past simple and present perfect in 3.6 B;
- use *for* and *since* correctly;
- use 10 of the 14 key words in her own sentence;
- write 12 sentences about her own experience with fewer than 4 tense errors.

**If it is too easy:** Lesson 5 goes to about 480 words, adds the present perfect continuous (*she has been studying*), and the comprehension set gains a second whole-passage question about the writer's attitude.
**If it is too hard:** keep the same passage for a second week, drop question 9, and drill only 3.1 and 3.4.

**A note on spaced recall.** `03-vocabulary.mp3` ends with five Lesson 2 words — *backup, folder, drive, explain, remember*. Lessons 2 and 3 both recalled Lesson 1, so Lesson 2's words have waited two lessons, which is exactly the gap this course keeps. Lesson 3's words are due back in Lesson 5.

segments.say: Slow version. The passage, read slowly, one time.

Lina is twenty-four. She lives in Gaza, and she has studied information technology at her college for three years. She has also done something her teachers never asked for: she has taught herself web design.

It started two years ago, with a free course on the internet. The course has more than forty lessons, and Lina has finished thirty-eight of them. She has never met her teacher. He lives in another country, and she has only seen his hands, moving on a keyboard, in short videos.

The connection in her building is slow, so she has learned to work in a careful way. She downloads a lesson at night, when the internet is quieter. She watches it in the morning, with no connection at all. She has lost her work many times, and now she saves every few minutes.

Her uncle has a small shop near the market. He has sold the same things for twenty years — bags, shoes, school things — and he has always sold them in the same way. People come to the shop, or they telephone him.

In March, Lina built a website for the shop. It is a simple one: four pages, some photographs, the prices, and a button that opens a message to her uncle's phone. She published it on a free service, because the shop has no money for anything else. It took her eleven days.

Since March, the shop has had customers from three other cities. They have never seen the shop, and they will probably never see it. They found the website, they looked at the prices, and they sent a message. Two of them have ordered from the shop more than once.

Her uncle has not learned to use a computer, and he does not want to. He has never used email. But he has asked Lina for two new pages, and he has started to say "my website" when he talks to his friends.

Lina has not finished the course yet. Two lessons are left, and they are the hardest ones. She has already decided what she will build after them: an account system, so that a customer can see what he has ordered before.

She says the same thing to every student who asks her how to begin. "I have not done anything big," she says. "I have done one small thing, many times, for two years".
